interviewQuestions.question: A region just went dark — walk me through what happens to in-flight traffic?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd split this into three groups of traffic instead of describing failover as one event. First, requests already mid-flight to the dead region: those don't reroute, they simply time out, and the client has to detect that and retry — so I'd check what retry logic exists on the client today. Second, new DNS lookups after the region fails: if health-based routing is wired up, those should stop resolving to the dead region within roughly a health-check interval plus TTL. Third, and the one people forget, clients that already cached a DNS answer for the dead region before it failed — they keep sending new requests there until their own cache expires, regardless of what I do on the server side, and some resolvers hold on well past the TTL I set.

I'd close by naming the actual numbers: health check interval, TTL, and an estimate of how long that third group persists, since that's the honest answer to "how long is the outage," not just "when did we update DNS."

**Testing:** whether you understand failover as staged across connection state, not an instantaneous cutover.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: What happens to in-flight traffic on failover

interviewQuestions.question: When would you reach for anycast instead of DNS-based geo-routing?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd reach for anycast when failover speed and uniformity across all clients matter more than operational simplicity — specifically when I can't tolerate the uneven, cache-dependent failover window that DNS-based routing has, where some clients reroute in seconds and others take minutes depending on resolver behavior. Anycast reroutes at the network layer via BGP, so it applies consistently to essentially all traffic on a similar timescale.

The catch is that anycast needs BGP-level control, which most application teams don't have directly — in practice I'd get it through a CDN or specialized network provider rather than running it myself. For a typical product team without that infrastructure relationship, I'd stick with DNS-based routing plus aggressive health checks and accept the imperfect failover window; I'd only push for anycast if the business case for sub-minute, uniform failover justified taking on that provider relationship.

**Testing:** whether you know anycast's advantage is real but comes with an infrastructure dependency most teams don't already have.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Anycast vs DNS-based routing

interviewQuestions.question: How would you design health checks so a region gets pulled out of rotation before users notice?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start by rejecting a shallow check — pinging the load balancer only proves the load balancer is up, not that the region can actually serve real traffic. I'd design the check to exercise a representative path: hit an endpoint that touches the database or a critical dependency, not just a static health route, so a region with a dead downstream dependency still gets marked unhealthy.

Then I'd tune the interval and failure threshold as a deliberate trade-off: checking every few seconds with a low failure threshold detects problems fast but risks flapping on transient blips, so I'd require a couple of consecutive failures before pulling the region, and pair that with a low DNS TTL so the removal actually reaches new lookups quickly. I'd also make sure the health check runs from outside the region itself, so a region that can't be reached externally still gets detected even if its internal checks report healthy.

**Testing:** whether you can design a health check that reflects real user-facing health, not just process liveness.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Designing health-based routing
